mcqs.question: A commit has already been pushed and teammates have pulled it. What determines whether `git reset` is safe to use here?
options: It's always safe, since reset only affects your local branch pointer
It's unsafe — once a commit is shared, reset removing it from your branch creates a divergence for everyone who already has it; revert is the safe option instead
Reset is safe as long as you also run `git push --force` immediately after
It depends only on whether the commit introduced a bug
mcqs.explanation: Reset rewrites which commits your branch points to, so removing an already-shared commit leaves everyone else's copy pointing at history your branch no longer has — revert instead adds a new commit undoing the change, which is safe precisely because it never removes anything. Force-pushing doesn't make reset safe, it's what actually propagates the unsafe rewrite to everyone else.

mcqs.question: You want to undo your last two commits but keep all their changes staged, ready to be recommitted as one cleaner commit. Which reset mode does that?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~2
git reset --mixed HEAD~2
git reset --soft HEAD~2
git revert HEAD~2
mcqs.explanation: --soft only moves HEAD, leaving the undone commits' changes sitting staged exactly as requested. --mixed would unstage them instead, --hard would also wipe them from the working directory entirely, and revert adds new commits rather than removing the existing ones from the branch.

mcqs.question: After running `git revert a1b2c3d`, what does the repository's history look like?
options: Commit a1b2c3d is removed as if it never existed
Commit a1b2c3d is rewritten in place with the opposite changes
A brand-new commit is added whose diff is the exact inverse of a1b2c3d, with the original commit still present in history
The branch pointer moves backward to the commit before a1b2c3d
mcqs.explanation: Revert is purely additive — it creates a new commit undoing the target's changes, leaving the original commit and everything after it untouched in history. Removing, rewriting in place, or moving the branch pointer backward are all reset-style behaviors, not what revert does.

mcqs.question: A bad commit is only on your own local branch, never pushed. Which tool is the simpler, more direct fix — reset or revert?
options: Revert, because it's the only safe option in any situation
Reset, because nobody else has the commit, so rewriting the branch to remove it cleanly is both safe and simpler than adding an inverse commit
Neither works on a purely local, unpushed commit
Revert, because reset cannot operate on unpushed commits
mcqs.explanation: When a commit is entirely local, reset can remove it outright with no risk to anyone else, which is simpler than revert's approach of adding a new undo commit on top. Reset works fine on unpushed commits — that's actually its ideal use case — and revert isn't the only safe option once nothing is shared yet.

mcqs.question: You accidentally deleted a branch that had commits not merged anywhere else. What's the correct recovery approach, assuming git hasn't garbage-collected yet?
options: The commits are permanently lost the moment the branch is deleted
Find the commit's hash in `git reflog`, then create a new branch pointing at that hash
Re-clone the repository from the remote to restore the branch
Run `git fetch --all` to pull the branch back down automatically
mcqs.explanation: Deleting a branch only removes the pointer, not the commit objects themselves — the reflog still records where HEAD was, so recreating a branch at that hash restores full access to the commit chain. Re-cloning or fetching won't help for commits that were never pushed, and the commits aren't permanently lost until gc actually prunes them.

mcqs.question: Why can't the reflog help recover work lost to `git reset --hard` on uncommitted changes?
options: The reflog only tracks commit objects, and uncommitted edits were never committed, so no commit ever existed for it to point back to
The reflog is disabled by default and must be manually enabled
reset --hard clears the reflog itself as part of running
The reflog only stores the five most recent actions
mcqs.explanation: The reflog is a log of where HEAD (and branches) have pointed across commits — it has nothing to reference for changes that were never committed in the first place. It isn't disabled by default, reset doesn't clear it, and its default retention window is far longer than five entries.
